According to the *{{ill|Wakan Sansai Zue|es|Wakan Sansai Zue|ff|Wakan Sansai Zue|fr|Wakan sansai zue|ja|和漢三才図会|ko|화한삼재도회|ru|Вакан сансай дзуэ|uk|Вакан сансай дзуе|vi|Wakan Sansai Zue|zh|和漢三才圖會|qid=Q1135803}}*, the enshrined deity is described as “Katte-sha: one enshrined deity, Aiman-no-Mikoto<ref>{{Cite web|Japanese book| url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/2569751 | title=Wakan Sansai Zue: 105 volumes, front 1 volume, end 1 volume [55] | work=National Diet Library Digital Collection | accessdate=2018-10-27}}</ref> (Ukeri-no-Mikoto / Ukenori-no-Mikoto).” It is also written as “Ukeman-no-Mikoto”<ref>{{Cite web|Japanese book| url=http://www.shiga-jinjacho.jp/ycBBS/Board.cgi/02_jinja_db/db/ycDB_02jinja-pc-detail.html?mode:view=1&view:oid=668 | title=Shrine Introduction > Shrines of Shiga Prefecture | work=Shiga Prefecture Association of Shinto Shrines | accessdate=2018-10-27}}</ref>. The current principal enshrined deity is said to be {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Ame-no-Oshihomimi-no-Mikoto}}. {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Ōyama-tsumi-no-Mikoto}}, {{ill|Kukunochi|de|Kukunoshi|es|Kukunochi|it|Kukunochi|ja|ククノチ|zh|久久能智|qid=Q10749920|lt=Kukunochi-no-Mikoto}}, {{ill|Konohanasakuya-hime|Q1781862|qid=Q1781862|lt=Konohanasakuya-hime-no-Mikoto}}, {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Koke-mushi-no-Mikoto}}, and {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Hano-hime-no-Mikoto}} are also enshrined together.

=== Overview ===
It is one of the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Yoshino Hassha Myōjin}}, guardian shrines of {{ill|Mount Ōmine|Q3695989|qid=Q3695989}} in Yoshino, and was formerly called “'''Katte Myōjin'''.” {{ill|Mount Aonegamine|Q11661968|qid=Q11661968}}, which corresponds to the source of the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Yoshino River}}, has been revered since ancient times as a {{ill|Suijin|Q3137449|qid=Q3137449}}. Accordingly, {{ill|Kinpu Shrine (Q3197197)|Q3197197|qid=Q3197197|lt=Kinpusen Shrine}} was built near the summit (Oku-Senbon), {{ill|Yoshino Mikumari Shrine|Q3529714|qid=Q3529714}} on the mountainside (Kami-Senbon), and Katte Shrine at the mountain’s foot (Naka-Senbon)<ref>“The History of Popular Salvation and Buddhism (Vol. 2)” by Munetoshi Nakaya, Ikuhōsha, 2012</ref>. “Katte” is also said to mean “entrance” or “lower side,” and from its written form it came to be worshipped as a deity of contests and as a {{ill|Military god|Q11637440|qid=Q11637440|lt=god of battle}}. During the period of {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|de|Shinbutsu-Shūgō|es|Shinbutsu shūgō|eu|Shinbutsu-shūgō|fa|شینبوتسو-شوگو|fi|Shinbutsu shūgō|fr|Shinbutsu shūgō|id|Shinbutsu-shūgō|it|Shinbutsu shūgō|ja|神仏習合|ko|신불습합|pl|Synkretyzm shintō-buddyjski|ru|Синто-буддийский синкретизм|th|ชิมบุตสึชูโง|tr|Şinbutsu-şuugō|uk|Синто-буддистський синкретизм|ur|شنتو اور بدھ مت کا امتزاج ضدین|zh|神佛習合|qid=Q2279088}} (the syncretism of Shinto and Buddhism), the honji (original Buddhist identity) of Katte Daimyōjin was said to be {{ill|Vaiśravaṇa|Q866315|qid=Q866315}}, leading to even greater veneration by the warrior class. In addition, because it is located at the entrance to {{ill|Mount Yoshino|arz|جبل مونت يوشينو|ca|Muntanya Yoshino|ceb|Yoshino Yama|cs|Jošino (hora)|de|Yoshino-yama|es|Monte Yoshino|eu|Yoshino mendia|fa|کوه یوشینو|fi|Yoshinovuori|fr|Mont Yoshino|id|Gunung Yoshino|it|Monte Yoshino|ja|吉野山|ko|요시노산|lld|Mont Yoshino|lt|Jošino kalnai|tr|Yoshino Dağı|zh|吉野山|qid=Q1036938}}, it was also called Yamaguchi Shrine<ref>“Nara: A Grown-Up’s Walking Guide,” Seibido Publishing, 2010</ref>.

The date of foundation is unknown, but the *Nichiyūji Keitōki* records it as the 6th year of {{ill|Emperor Kōan|ar|الإمبراطور كوان|arz|الامبراطور كوان|azb|کوان (ایمپیراتور)|ca|Kōan|ckb|ئیمپراتۆر کۆوان|cs|Kóan (císař)|de|Kōan (Tennō)|eo|Koan|es|Kōan Tennō|fa|امپراتور کوآن|fi|Kōan (keisari)|fr|Kōan (empereur)|he|קואן, קיסר יפן|hr|Kōan (japanski car)|hu|Kóan japán császár|id|Kaisar Kōan|it|Kōan (imperatore del Giappone)|ja|孝安天皇|ka|კოანი|ko|고안 천황|lt|Imperatorius Koanas|ms|Maharaja Kōan|nl|Koan (keizer)|pl|Kōan|pt|Koan (imperador)|ru|Император Коан|sh|Car Kōan|simple|Emperor Kōan|sl|Cesar Koan|sr|Коан (јапански цар)|sv|Koan (kejsare)|th|จักรพรรดิโคอัง|tl|Emperador Koan|tr|Kōan (imparator)|uk|Імператор Коан|uz|Imperator Kōan|vi|Thiên hoàng Kōan|zh|孝安天皇|zh_min_nan|Kôan Thian-hông|zh_yue|孝安天皇|qid=Q312821}} ({{ill|386 BC|ab|Ҳ. ҟ. 386|ar|386 ق م|ary|386 قبل لميلاد|arz|386 ق م|ast|386 e.C.|az|E.ə. 386|be_x_old|386 да н. э.|bs|386. p. n. e.|ca|386 aC|cs|386 př. n. l.|cy|386 CC|da|386 f.Kr.|de|386 v. It is said that when {{ill|Emperor Tenmu|Q335181|qid=Q335181|lt=Prince Ōama}} played the koto in the shrine hall, {{ill|Celestial maiden|Q111467505|qid=Q111467505}} descended and danced, waving their sleeves five times. The mountain behind the shrine came to be called “Sodefuri-yama” (Sleeve-Waving Mountain). This legend is also said to be the origin of the court dance known as “{{ill|Gosechi no Mai|Q11372604|qid=Q11372604}}”<ref name="yoshimizu" />.

Within the precincts remains a dance mound said to mark the spot where {{ill|Shizuka Gozen|Q3088217|qid=Q3088217}}, the wife of {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshitsune|Q310445|qid=Q310445}}, performed a dance when she was captured by pursuers. The {{ill|Honden|Q2044994|qid=Q2044994}}, built in the {{ill|Nagare-zukuri|fr|Nagare-zukuri|it|Nagare-zukuri|ja|流造|pl|Nagare-zukuri|ru|Нагарэ-дзукури|sv|Nagare-zukuri|zh|流造|qid=Q210684}} style with a {{ill|cypress bark roof|Q90373477|qid=Q90373477}} roof, measuring eight bays by two bays, was designated a prefectural {{ill|Tangible Cultural Property (Japan)|Q2901860|qid=Q2901860}}. However, it was destroyed by suspected arson in {{ill|Heisei era|Q234510|qid=Q234510}} 13 ({{ill|2001|Q1988|qid=Q1988}}). The sacred object has since been transferred to the facing {{ill|Yoshimizu Shrine|Q3572667|qid=Q3572667}}, and donations are being solicited for the reconstruction of the main hall.

=== Relationship with Zao Gongen and Komori Myōjin ===
{{Multiple image
 | footer = Katte Myōjin (left) and Komori Myōjin (right) as depicted in the Yoshino Mandala
 | image1 = Katte-Myojin.jpg
 | image2 = Komori-Myojin.jpg
 | total_width = 350
}}
{{ill|Zaō Gongen|Q10514059|qid=Q10514059}} ({{ill|Kimpusen-ji|Q1741668|qid=Q1741668}}), Komori Gongen (Yoshino Mikumari Shrine), and Katte Gongen (Katte Shrine) were enshrined together as the Three Gongen at {{ill|Hōki Province|Q1053703|qid=Q1053703|lt=Sanbutsu-ji in Hōki Province}}. Zao Gongen was enshrined at the inner sanctuary ({{ill|Nageire-dō|Q19826408|qid=Q19826408}}), Komori Gongen at the Jizō Hall, and Katte Gongen at the Monju Hall<ref name="tottori">{{Cite web|Japanese book|date=2007-12-26| url=https://www.pref.tottori.lg.jp/secure/224955/02-1bunkazaiseirihyou.pdf | title=“Proposal for Assets Listed on the Tentative List of World Heritage Sites”: Cultural Properties Included in the Assets (5-1) Inventory Table | work=Official Tottori Prefecture Website | accessdate=2013-04-15}}</ref>. Katte Myōjin was also enshrined independently at shrines throughout the country and serves as the head shrine of 28 Katte Shrines nationwide<ref name="yoshimizu">{{Cite web|Japanese book| url=http://www.yoshimizu-shrine.com/pdf/syuisho.pdf | title=Prospectus for Support of Katte Shrine Reconstruction | work=Official Website of Yoshimizu Shrine | accessdate=2013-04-10|archive-url=https://www.web.archive.org/web/20060219194625/http://www.yoshimizu-shrine.com:80/pdf/syuisho.pdf |archive-date=2006-02-19 |url-status=dead |url-status-date=2024-09-21}}</ref>.

Komori Myōjin, the enshrined deity of Yoshino Mikumari Shrine, is said to be the consort deity of Katte Myōjin, with Katte Myōjin as the male deity and Komori Myōjin as the female deity. In the Noh play “{{ill|Arashiyama|Q17988500|qid=Q17988500|lt=Arashiyama}},” which was established in the late Muromachi period, an elderly couple who serve as guardians of the cherry blossoms of {{ill|Arashiyama|Q2859566|qid=Q2859566}}—transplanted from Yoshino—are revealed to be manifestations of the deities Katte and Komori. The play’s plot proclaims that Zao Gongen, Katte Myōjin, and Komori Myōjin are three aspects of a single divine entity<ref>{{Cite web || url=http://www.tessen.org/dictionary/explain/arashiyama/ | title=Arashiyama | work=Tessenkai Noh Theatre Dictionary | accessdate=2013-04-09}}</ref>.
